name: POLR3-related (4H) leukodystrophy
aliases: hypomyelination with hypodontia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy caused by variants in subunits of RNA polymerase III, most often POLR3A or POLR3B, and less commonly POLR1C
The classic clinical triad giving the name 4H is Hypomyelination, Hypodontia and Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, though not every child shows all three
Neurological features include cerebellar signs with ataxia and intention tremor, a tremor-ataxia presentation, spasticity, and often myopia and abnormal eye movements
Dental clues are valuable: delayed or abnormal dentition, missing teeth, an abnormal eruption sequence and occasionally natal teeth

The MRI pattern combines diffuse hypomyelination with cerebellar atrophy and relative T2 hypointensity (preservation) of specific structures such as the optic radiations, the anterolateral thalamus, the globus pallidus, the dentate nucleus and the corticospinal tracts within the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Endocrine involvement causes delayed, incomplete or absent puberty from hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and warrants specialist assessment

Diagnosis follows MRI pattern recognition and characteristic dental and endocrine findings, confirmed by POLR3A/POLR3B/POLR1C sequencing; management is supportive with hormone replacement and multidisciplinary rehabilitation
reference.pathophysiology: POLR3-related leukodystrophy results from biallelic variants in genes encoding subunits of RNA polymerase III, the enzyme that transcribes small non-coding RNAs such as transfer RNAs and 5S ribosomal RNA. Impaired polymerase III activity is thought to reduce the supply of these RNAs needed for efficient protein synthesis, disproportionately affecting cells with high biosynthetic demands, including oligodendrocytes during myelination. The consequent failure of adequate myelin deposition produces hypomyelination, while involvement of other tissues explains the dental, endocrine and ocular manifestations that accompany the neurological picture.
additionalDifferentials: Other RNA polymerase-related and tRNA-processing hypomyelinating disorders
Fucosidosis and other storage disorders with hypomyelination
Congenital cerebellar ataxias with white matter change
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to identify hypomyelination with cerebellar atrophy and the pattern of selectively preserved T2-hypointense structures
Sequencing of POLR3A, POLR3B and POLR1C, with panel or exome analysis if targeted testing is negative
Dental and orthopantomogram assessment to document hypodontia and abnormal dentition
Endocrine evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and pubertal status
Ophthalmological review for myopia and eye-movement abnormalities
Growth monitoring and assessment for short stature
redFlags: Failure of pubertal progression requiring endocrine intervention
Rapid neurological deterioration inconsistent with the usually slow course, prompting reassessment
Dysphagia with aspiration risk as bulbar involvement advances
Recurrent falls and injury from worsening ataxia and spasticity
reference.prognosis: POLR3-related leukodystrophy is usually slowly progressive; many children develop skills before plateauing and then declining, with gait, coordination and speech becoming increasingly affected over years. Severity varies widely with genotype, from relatively mild adolescent-onset forms to more severe early-onset disease, and prognosis is influenced by the degree of motor and bulbar involvement.
pitfalls: Not recognising the specific pattern of preserved T2-hypointense structures that distinguishes this from other hypomyelinating disorders
Overlooking dental and endocrine clues that strongly support the diagnosis
Failing to screen for and treat hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, affecting puberty and bone health
Assuming a static encephalopathy and not pursuing leukodystrophy genetics
Neglecting genetic counselling for autosomal recessive recurrence risk
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is multidisciplinary and supportive, coordinated by neurology and clinical genetics
Hormone replacement for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism to induce and maintain puberty, with endocrine surveillance of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
Dental assessment and management of hypodontia and abnormal dentition
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy with treatment of spasticity and ataxia, and mobility aids as disability progresses
Symptomatic and antiepileptic treatment as neurological features evolve, with speech and swallowing support
Ophthalmology review with correction of myopia and management of eye-movement abnormalities
Genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder, with carrier testing and reproductive counselling for the family
